blocks.text: You can integrate AI Security with the Amazon Security Lake service to export and store the alert data in a dedicated Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) bucket that is pre-configured as part of the Amazon Security Lake setup.

Amazon Security Lake is a data lake for security logs, built into the customer’s account. The data lake is backed by an Amazon S3 bucket and organizes data as a set of Lake Formation tables. Amazon Security Lake is designed to optimize the cost of storing and querying massive security logs. Amazon Security Lake uses the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) as the selected format for the alert information and requires the Parquet file format for the stored alerts. To learn more, refer to the AWS documentation.
Complete the following steps before exporting the alert data to Amazon Security Lake:

blocks.item: 1. Configure the Amazon Security Lake service.
Make sure you have a configured Amazon Security Lake service that is connected to an S3 bucket in your AWS account. To learn more, refer to the Amazon Security Lake documentation.
2. Configure the custom source.

Zscaler is regarded as a source integration for Amazon Security Lake. To enable the integration, you must generate a custom source in Amazon Security Lake. To learn more, refer to the Amazon Security Lake documentation.
Sign in to your AWS account.
Open the Security Lake console.
From the Security Lake left-side navigation, select customized sources.
Scroll down to the Customized source details section:

Data source name: Provide a name for this custom source. This name determines the path in the S3 bucket to which the alert data is written. Amazon Security Lake generates a new folder for each custom source.
Event class: Make sure you use the Security_Finding event class.

Region: Select the region from the drop-down menu. The custom source is created in the region where the AWS console is connected. You need to specify this region while setting up the Security Lake integration in the AI Security Admin Portal.
Account ID: Enter the account ID that you copied from the Cloud Storage page in the AI Security Admin Portal.
External ID: Enter the external ID that you copied from the Cloud Storage page in the AI Security Admin Portal. To learn more, refer to the AWS documentation.
The AWS Account ID and External ID are identifiers of the custom source (AI Security) that writes logs and events to the data lake.
See image.
Click Create.
The Amazon Security Lake custom source is created.
On the Customized sources page, search for the custom source you created.
Copy the ARN IAM role. You need to provide this value while setting up the Security Lake integration in the AI Security Admin Portal.
See image.
3. Collect the S3 Bucket details.
Make sure you have the following information for setting up the AI Security integration:
The Amazon Security Lake S3 region.
The S3 bucket name (e.g., aws-security-data-lake-us-east-2-o-4g8wg3sx9z).
The folder prefix for the custom source path on the S3 bucket (e.g., /ext/dspm-security-alerts).

blocks.heading: Integrating AI Security with Amazon Security Lake

blocks.text: To configure the Amazon Security Lake integration:

blocks.item: Go to Administration > External Integrations.
Click Add for cloud storage integration.
On the Add Cloud Storage Integration page:
For Integration Name, enter a unique name for the integration.
For Cloud Storage, select Amazon Security Lake.
Click Next.
On the Cloud Storage page:
AI Security AWS Account: Copy the AI Security AWS Account ID and paste it in the Account ID field while creating the custom source on the Amazon Security Lake console.
External ID: Copy the External ID and paste it in the External ID field while creating the custom source on the Amazon Security Lake console.
IAM Role: Enter the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) ARN role that you copied after creating the custom source. This role allows the AI Security AWS account to write data to Security Lake.
Amazon S3 Bucket Name: Provide the Amazon S3 bucket name.
Bucket Region: Select the bucket region from the drop-down menu. You should have these details from the Prerequisites step.
Folder Location: Provide the folder path for the S3 bucket set for Amazon Security Lake. You should have these details from the Prerequisites step.
Click Test Connection to verify the connection between AI Security and the AWS service. The test connection validates that the S3 bucket exists.
A message is displayed that the connection is successful.
Click Next.
Review the integration summary. Click the Edit icon if you want to make any changes.
See image.
Click Finish.

blocks.text: You can see the integration details on the Integrations page. The initial status shows as Pending because data is not yet sent to the Amazon Security Lake. After you configure and associate the alert rules with this integration, and when AI Security starts sending the alert data to Amazon Security Lake, the status changes to Success.

Partitioning is a technique for organizing datasets, so they can be queried efficiently. AI Security alerts are exported in OCSF format to Amazon Security Lake and are stored in Parquet files. The Parquet format is a column-based data format.

The files are limited by size. A new file is generated and posted whenever the file size reaches 256 MB or after 5 minutes. The files are stored under the root path created for the custom source. The folder structure is: region=<awsregion>/accountid=<cloudaccountid>/eventDay=<YYYYMMDD>.
New folders are generated to host new alert files.

OCSF includes an open specification for the normalization of security telemetry across a wide range of security products and services, as well as open-source tools that provide support for using the OCSF schema. To learn more, refer to the GitHub page on OCSF.

blocks.item: Cloud alert data logs written to OCSF

blocks.text: Zscaler recommends the following resolutions for issues that you might encounter while integrating and using AI Security with Amazon Security Lake.

table: The AI Security alert data is available in the Amazon Security Lake S3 bucket, but the Glue Crawler fails to parse the data into Amazon Security Lake.
This issue typically occurs when the custom source that is created for the integration is using the wrong event class. Make sure you create the custom source with the Security Finding event class.
Amazon Security Lake integration object on the AI Security Integrations page shows a Failed status.

This indicates that AI Security does not have the permission to access the Amazon Security Lake S3 bucket. While integrating AI Security with Amazon Security Lake, make sure you have applied the required policy to grant AI Security access to the S3 bucket.
New alerts are present in the AI Security Admin Portal but are not exported into Amazon Security Lake.
Make sure you've configured the alert rule notification and check the scope of the alert rule.
